# Scaling Ion-Trap Quantum Computing from Demonstrations to Useful Fault-Tolerant Systems

As of 13 September 2026, the most credible route from ion-trap demonstrations to useful large-scale quantum computing is a layered combination: segmented quantum charge-coupled devices (QCCDs) with local ion shuttling, increasingly integrated electronic and photonic control, and error-correction codes designed together with the hardware. QCCD currently has the strongest demonstrated evidence for preserving high fidelity while increasing system size: Quantinuum’s Helios operates 98 physical barium-ion qubits with average two-qubit infidelity of $`7.9(2)\times10^{-4}`$ across its operational zones, while earlier experiments demonstrated fast, deterministic inter-module ion transport at 2,424 transfers per second with ion-loss infidelity below $`7\times10^{-8}`$ ([Nature’s Helios report](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10676-4); [Nature Communications matter-link experiment](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-35285-3)).

That result is not yet a utility-scale quantum computer. Remote photonic links, large-scale control, real-time decoding, manufacturing yield, and end-to-end logical workloads remain incomplete. Photonic interconnects are essential for systems larger than a practical QCCD module, but the best demonstrated trapped-ion links cited in the current literature reach about 97% fidelity at rates up to 250 pairs per second—far below the rate and fidelity required by many fault-tolerant architectures. A 2026 Bell-factory design projects 99.9%-fidelity remote pairs at $`10^5`$ pairs per second per square centimetre, but it is a model and excludes mapping the generated pair onto processor data qubits ([modular-entanglement Perspective](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.18387)).

The leading practical judgment is therefore conditional. QCCD with local shuttling is the most likely near-term physical backbone; electronic qubit control and trap-integrated photonics are the most promising ways to relieve its wiring and optical-control burdens; and qLDPC or related co-designed error-correction architectures may eventually provide the best logical-qubit density. Fixed photonic modules and distributed error correction are likely necessary for very large machines, but their quantitative link performance and data-qubit integration are not yet demonstrated at the required scale.

This report defines what “useful scale” means, catalogs current programs, compares the principal scaling strategies, examines the engineering barriers, maps architectures to workloads, and concludes with an evidence-weighted ranking and measurable milestones.

## 1. Scope, baseline, and the meaning of useful scale

### 1.1 The transition is not a qubit-count contest

The starting point is not one precise number. Historically, trapped-ion demonstrations involved tens of qubits. The National Academies described small gate-based demonstrations as systems “on the order of tens of qubits” and NISQ systems as machines with hundreds of physical but non-fault-tolerant qubits ([National Academies assessment](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/25196/chapter/9)). A 2022 modular-QCCD analysis similarly characterized the demonstrated trapped-ion baseline as “up to 10s of qubits,” while estimating that a single large fabricated array might contain approximately $`2.6\times10^4`$ qubits under aggressive geometric assumptions ([Nature Communications modular-QCCD study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-35285-3)).

The current hardware landscape has moved beyond that historical baseline, but the numbers are not directly interchangeable. Helios is reported in a primary Nature paper as a 98-qubit QCCD processor. Secondary sources list 48 or 94 logical qubits for Helios, depending on whether they count a particular code encoding, detected logical states, or another logical-qubit definition. IonQ systems are variously reported at 100 or 256 physical qubits depending on configuration and source. These figures describe different dates, device configurations, and measurement conventions; they do not form a clean leaderboard.

The relevant transition is from:

- a small or medium physical processor executing circuits directly on noisy qubits;
- to a machine containing many independently controllable processing, memory, cooling, measurement, and transport zones;
- to a fault-tolerant processor that executes long logical circuits with active error correction;
- and finally to a system whose complete workload beats a credible classical baseline on accuracy, time, cost, or energy.

A large physical array that cannot maintain uniform fidelity, calibrate itself, recover from ion loss, or supply enough syndrome measurements may be less useful than a smaller system with fewer but better logical qubits.

### 1.2 An operational definition of the endpoint

A large-scale ion-trap system should be considered capable of solving real-world problems only when it demonstrates all of the following at workload-relevant scale:

1. It maintains encoded logical qubits whose error per correction cycle is below the corresponding unencoded physical baseline.

2. It runs repeated error correction with real-time syndrome processing and feed-forward rather than relying on post-selection that discards unsuccessful executions.

3. It executes a logical circuit deep enough for the target application, including non-Clifford operations, state preparation, measurement, and classical control.

4. It reports application accuracy, wall-clock time, number of samples, classical baseline, total physical and logical resources, and failure probability.

5. It operates with an acceptable deployment model: predictable uptime, maintainable vacuum and optical systems, manageable power and cooling, recoverable component failures, and a sufficiently large trained workforce.

The Walking Cat architecture gives a useful workload-level distinction: NISQ systems can execute thousands of gates on hundreds of physical qubits, whereas utility-scale fault-tolerant computing is expected to require tens of millions of reliable gates on thousands of logical qubits ([Walking Cat architecture](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2604.19481)). The National Academies similarly described a general-purpose machine as one that could scale to many thousands of logical qubits with software capable of helping programmers use them.

This does not mean every useful application needs thousands of logical qubits. A smaller fault-tolerant machine might provide value in a specialized chemistry, materials, optimization, or sensing task. The endpoint is therefore workload-specific, but it must be defined by reliable logical computation and time-to-solution rather than physical-qubit count alone.

### 1.3 Metrics that distinguish progress from appearance

The most informative metrics fall into several layers.

| Layer | Required measurements | Why they matter |
|---|---|---|
| Physical device | Physical qubits, ion species, trap geometry, all-pairs or median 1Q/2Q fidelity, SPAM error, coherence, gate duration | Establishes raw hardware quality and whether performance survives across the device |
| Operations | Parallel two-qubit capacity, transport time, motional excitation, cooling time, crosstalk, calibration time, uptime | Determines actual circuit throughput rather than isolated gate performance |
| Logical processor | Logical-qubit count, code family, physical-to-logical overhead, logical error per cycle, QEC-cycle time, decoder and feed-forward latency | Measures fault-tolerant capability |
| Application | Circuit depth, logical gate counts, accuracy, shots, wall-clock time, classical baseline, time-to-solution | Tests whether the system solves a meaningful problem |
| Deployment | Power, footprint, cost, maintenance interval, staffing, supply chain, serviceability, cloud or on-premises access | Determines whether the system can be operated outside a specialized laboratory |

A single metric is inadequate. Quantum volume, algorithmic-qubit scores, peak two-qubit fidelity, and raw physical-qubit count each capture only part of the system. An application-oriented benchmarking study warns that neither quantum volume nor any other single metric reliably predicts performance across all workloads because crosstalk, routing, circuit shape, and software overhead are omitted ([application-oriented benchmarking study](https://doi.org/10.1109/tqe.2023.3253761)).

The National Academies proposed two complementary scaling measures: physical-qubit doubling time at a fixed average gate error, followed by effective logical-qubit count and logical-qubit doubling time once error correction becomes effective. That distinction remains useful. Physical scaling matters for building the platform; logical scaling determines when the platform can execute useful algorithms.

### 1.4 Historical developments that explain the current choices

The modern scaling debate follows a clear sequence.

| Period | Principal development | Transition it enabled |
|---|---|---|
| 2002 | Kielpinski, Monroe, and Wineland proposed the QCCD architecture, separating memory, processing, and transport zones | Replaced the assumption that all ions must remain in one crystal |
| 2014 | Modular ion-trap architecture with local atomic interactions and probabilistic photonic links showed a fault-tolerant hierarchy | Established photonic networking as the long-range scaling route |
| 2021–2023 | Experimental QCCD systems demonstrated multiple zones, transport, mid-circuit measurement, teleported gates, and the Race-Track processor | Turned QCCD from an architectural proposal into a working processor design |
| 2022 | Deterministic inter-module ion transport reached 2,424 transfers per second with extremely low transport-loss error | Supplied a practical short-range modular link |
| 2023–2025 | Grid traps, integrated photonics, optical-tweezer segmentation, and all-electronic control addressed wiring and parallelism | Shifted the problem from basic qubit quality toward integration |
| 2026 | Helios, early repeated QEC, distributed error detection, qLDPC blueprints, and Bell-factory proposals connected hardware to fault-tolerant system designs | Made cross-layer co-design the central scaling question |

The important transition is from “make one crystal larger” to “compose specialized modules.” Single crystals retain valuable all-to-all connectivity, but collective motional modes, control complexity, and decreasing gate speed make indefinite growth unattractive. QCCD, fixed photonic modules, and hybrid networks all preserve the high fidelity of small local registers by moving either ions or entanglement between specialized regions.

### 1.5 Evidence status

The evidence in this field belongs to four different categories:

- **Measured:** an experimental result on a specified device, such as Helios’s component infidelities or UQConnect’s transport fidelity.
- **Modeled:** a simulation, resource estimate, or architecture calculation, such as the Walking Cat workload estimates.
- **Projected:** a proposed performance level using assumed future components, such as the Bell-factory rate density.
- **Roadmap:** a company or program target, such as a planned 10,000-qubit processor.

These categories cannot be combined as if they were equivalent. A roadmap can identify a strategic direction, but it does not demonstrate feasibility. A resource estimate can reveal the required engineering target, but it does not demonstrate that the target machine can be built.

## 2. Current demonstrations and named scaling programs

### 2.1 Quantinuum: the strongest current QCCD evidence

Quantinuum’s program is the clearest example of a commercial QCCD trajectory. Its H2 systems use a racetrack-style architecture with memory and processing regions, ion transport, and all-to-all logical connectivity within the active register. H2-1 was announced in 2024 as a 56-trapped-ion processor. A joint Quantinuum–JPMorgan Chase random-circuit-sampling experiment reported a substantial improvement over the 2019 Google benchmark, but this was a cross-entropy benchmark rather than a general real-world workload ([H2-1 announcement](https://www.quantinuum.com/press-releases/quantinuum-launches-industry-first-trapped-ion-56-qubit-quantum-computer-that-challenges-the-worlds-best-supercomputers)).

An earlier 32-qubit Quantinuum machine produced four highly reliable logical qubits through Microsoft’s qubit-virtualization system. The result demonstrated that error correction could yield a useful logical object, but the accompanying claim that larger machines would produce more and better logical qubits was forward-looking at the time.

The 2026 Nature report on Helios is more consequential physically. Helios contains 98 $`^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^+`$ hyperfine qubits. A rotatable storage ring and junction connect two quantum-operation regions, separating memory from logic while preserving all-to-all connectivity. Its logic region processes batches of up to 16 qubits using eight operation zones; two-qubit operations are available in four of those zones. This is a concrete answer to the problem of preventing a single long chain from carrying every operation ([Helios hardware report](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10676-4)).

The measured component infidelities, averaged across operational zones, are:

- single-qubit gates: $`2.5(1)\times10^{-5}`$;
- two-qubit gates: $`7.9(2)\times10^{-4}`$;
- state preparation and measurement: $`3.3(5)\times10^{-4}`$.

These are strong numbers, but they are component averages, not a complete fault-tolerant application result. Helios also exposes the QCCD throughput problem. In a representative depth-ten random-pairing program, the average depth-one layer took approximately 55 milliseconds; a two-qubit gate took approximately 70 microseconds, and extra cooling after a transport operation took approximately 300 microseconds. Feed-forward can save several milliseconds in sorting, while measurement-conditioned operations add submillisecond latency, but the system-level clock remains much slower than the isolated gate time.

Logical-qubit counts reported for Helios must be treated carefully. Secondary sources describe 48 logical qubits using “Skinny Logic” at a 2:1 physical-to-logical ratio, while Quantum Ledger lists 94 demonstrated logical qubits associated with a different error-detection or encoding claim. The primary Nature hardware paper establishes the 98-physical-qubit processor and its component performance but does not provide a matching, universally defined logical-qubit count. As Quantum Ledger correctly warns, a distance-seven surface-code qubit, a Steane-code qubit, and an Iceberg-detected qubit are not interchangeable ([Quantum Ledger scorecard](https://quantumledger.report/benchmarks)). The correct conclusion is that Helios has demonstrated important early logical capabilities, not that “94 logical qubits” is a directly comparable universal quantity.

Quantinuum’s next steps combine hardware, QEC, and manufacturing. A September 2026 release describes a $100 million U.S. Department of Commerce CHIPS R&D award, with GlobalFoundries working on 300-millimetre-wafer fabrication for ion traps and electronics and Monarch Quantum working on scalable lasers and optical components ([CHIPS manufacturing award](https://www.quantinuum.com/press-releases/quantinuum-finalizes-100-million-chips-r-d-award-with-u-s-department-of-commerce-to-advance-trapped-ion-quantum-computer-manufacturing-in-the-us)). This is strategically important because it treats ion-trap hardware as a manufacturing problem rather than a sequence of bespoke optical experiments. It is not yet evidence of production yield: die sizes, wafer starts, process geometry, expected yield, and the date of first operational foundry-produced hardware have not been disclosed ([manufacturing analysis](https://www.inelectronics.co.uk/quantinuum-moves-quantum-hardware-onto-300mm-manufacturing/)).

Quantinuum and Microsoft also report a 12-logical-qubit chemistry workflow using active syndrome extraction, AI, and HPC resources. More than 14,000 individual experiments were reported without an observed error in one milestone. A related account of the peer-reviewed experiment notes that some reduced-error demonstrations used scalable post-selection and that full real-time decoding was not implemented; this is therefore meaningful logical-QEC evidence, but not yet a complete commercial fault-tolerant machine ([Microsoft chemistry and QEC report](https://quantum.microsoft.com/en-us/insights/blogs/microsoft-application-of-error-correction-to-trapped-ion-qubits); [Nature result and limitations](https://gcn.com/peer-reviewed-data-published-nature-confirms/21532/)).

A September 2026 C4-Helix preprint reports a more direct active-QEC experiment on Helios. It measured repeated-QEC error of $`4.6^{+6.2}_{-2.6}\times10^{-5}`$ per logical qubit per QEC cycle, complete-Clifford error of $`2.8^{+1.0}_{-1.6}\times10^{-4}`$ per two-qubit logical Clifford, and a three-logical-qubit GHZ-state fidelity lower bound of $`99.925^{+0.068}_{-0.245}\%`$, without postselection. These are important early-fault-tolerance results, but the experiments cover a single code block and a three-logical-qubit state rather than a large logical processor ([C4-Helix preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03194)).

### 2.2 IonQ: reconfigurable multicore, electronic control, and qLDPC

IonQ’s scaling strategy begins with the observation that a single long chain eventually becomes difficult to control. Its Reconfigurable Multicore Quantum Architecture (RMQA) uses multiple shorter chains that can be combined into highly connected cores or operated in parallel. An illustrative RMQA configuration uses four chains of 16 ions, with 12 computing ions and four refrigerant ions per chain; combining chains yields a 32-ion core and an example with 48 highly connected qubits. IonQ presents this as a foundation for triple-digit qubit systems and later multicore processors, but the cited technology demonstrator does not supply a complete measured system matrix for fidelity, transport latency, or parallel throughput ([RMQA description](https://www.ionq.com/resources/reconfigurable-multicore-quantum-architecture)).

IonQ’s Forte illustrates both the strengths and limitations of the single-chain route. A 2024 peer-reviewed benchmark used a 30-qubit single-chain processor with all-to-all operations and direct randomized benchmarking across all $`30\choose2=435`$ qubit pairs. The system reached an application-oriented algorithmic-qubit score of #AQ 29 ([Forte benchmark](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2024-11-07-1516/)). IonQ’s product material separately lists a 36-physical-qubit Forte configuration with approximately 0.02% single-qubit error, 0.4% two-qubit error, and 0.5% SPAM error under its stated protocols ([IonQ Forte specifications](https://www.ionq.com/quantum-systems/forte)).

The Forte benchmark also illustrates why scaling cannot rely only on component characterization. Its system-level model correlated with experiment but quantitatively overpredicted application-circuit performance because of errors outside the model. The authors explicitly note that characterization becomes more difficult as systems grow larger and higher quality. This is a warning against extrapolating an isolated peak fidelity to a complete processor.

IonQ is also pursuing electronic or semiconductor-integrated control. The approach replaces individually addressed gate beams with microwave and radio-frequency fields delivered through electrodes or antennas integrated into the trap, while retaining optical systems for cooling, preparation, and measurement. Company and secondary reports cite approximately 99.99% two-qubit fidelity in prototypes and targets for 256-qubit and 10,000-plus-qubit systems, but the survival of that fidelity across a production-scale device remains unproven ([IonQ roadmap account](https://www.roic.ai/quote/IONQ/transcripts/2026-year/2-quarter); [systems-integration guide](https://postquantum.com/building-quantum-computers/building-trapped-ion-quantum-computer/)).

IonQ’s Walking Cat architecture is a more complete logical proposal. It combines moving-ion QCCD hardware, cat-state factories, quantum LDPC codes, a compiler, a microarchitecture, and a streaming decoder. Its dense $`[[102,22,9]]`$ code encodes 22 logical qubits in 102 physical code qubits in the model, compared with 1,782 physical qubits for a surface-code implementation of the same 22 logical qubits and minimum distance. A modeled configuration uses 2,514 physical qubits for 110 logical qubits and approximately one million T gates per day at a target logical error rate of $`10^{-10}`$.

These are not measurements from a 2,514-qubit processor. The architecture assumes physical two-qubit error around $`10^{-4}`$, specific leakage and loss rates, transport times, decoder performance, code layouts, and QCCD operations. Its value is that it exposes a complete cross-layer design and identifies the hardware requirements that must be built. It is stronger evidence than a high-level qubit-count projection, but weaker evidence than an operational fault-tolerant machine.

IonQ also published an end-to-end resource estimate for Shor’s algorithm on the 256-bit secp256k1 elliptic-curve discrete-log problem. The estimate uses approximately 1,450 logical qubits, 40 million Toffoli gates, 19,397 physical qubits, 25.7 days per attempt, and an estimated 63% success probability. The underlying logical-level success bound has confidence at least $`1-2^{-128}`$, but the 63% figure is the heuristic physical-system estimate; neither is an experimental probability from a deployed machine ([ECDLP resource estimate](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1916)). This is a concrete target for system design, not a demonstrated cryptanalytic capability.

### 2.3 Oxford Ionics: electronic qubit control on a multi-zone chip

Oxford Ionics provides the strongest experimentally reported evidence for all-electronic gate control in a multi-zone ion trap. Its Electronic Qubit Control (EQC) approach integrates control electrodes onto a silicon trap and uses microwave or radio-frequency fields for gates, reducing dependence on individually aligned laser beams.

A 2025 PRX Quantum experiment demonstrated low-noise, site-selective single- and two-qubit gates in a seven-zone microfabricated trap. It reported average two-qubit entanglement fidelity of $`99.97(1)\%`$ and average single-qubit fidelity of at least $`99.99912(8)\%`$ while switching the interaction on in one zone and off in the others ([all-electronic control experiment](https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/h4wk-v31j)). The experiment establishes local selectivity and good fidelity, but it does not demonstrate a 256-qubit or 10,000-qubit processor.

Oxford Ionics’ roadmap places Foundation systems at 16–64 qubits and 99.99% fidelity, Enterprise systems at 256 qubits and 99.99% fidelity, and a 10,000-plus-qubit “Value at scale” processor in a 2027 target phase. The company also reports more than $20 million in 2024 sales and deployment of a full-stack QUARTET system at the UK National Quantum Computing Centre. These facts demonstrate early commercialization and deployment capability, not fault tolerance at the proposed scale ([Oxford Ionics roadmap](https://www.oxionics.com/announcements/oxford-ionics-unveils-development-roadmap-to-scalable-fault-tolerant-quantum-computing/); [QUARTET deployment](https://www.oxionics.com/announcements/oxford-ionics-delivers-quantum-computer-to-the-uks-national-quantum-computing-centre/)).

The central question for EQC is whether the control advantage survives scale. Radio-frequency fields are easier to distribute than individually addressed laser beams, but they are less spatially selective. The system must control crosstalk, RF amplitude and phase, antenna variation, ion positioning, thermal dissipation, and compatibility between electrode layers and vacuum materials. The seven-zone result is an important primitive; it is not yet a system-level scaling law.

### 2.4 Universal Quantum and DLR: low-temperature modular silicon traps

Universal Quantum and the German Aerospace Center’s Quantum Computing Initiative provide a different modular route. The Toccata project combines silicon ion-trap chips, global microwave fields, an ASIC with low-noise DACs, active error correction, and module networking. Its initial design targets at least 50 or 100 qubits, with several hundred through module networking and an eventual architectural extension to millions. The system is described as operating near 70 K rather than at the near-absolute-zero temperatures used by many other platforms ([DLR Toccata](https://qci.dlr.de/en/toccata/); [Universal Quantum–DLR architecture](https://universalquantum.com/knowledge-hub/development-of-a-scalable-user-friendly-quantum-processor-with-ion-trap-technology-for-dlr-qci)).

The distinguishing interconnect is UQConnect, an electronic matter link that moves ions between neighboring chips within a shared extreme-high-vacuum environment. Universal Quantum reports 2,424 connections per second and 99.999993% transmission fidelity, with a development path involving four modules, initially containing at least ten qubits each and potentially more than 25 qubits per module.

This result is valuable, but it must not be confused with remote photonic entanglement. UQConnect transfers physical ions deterministically over a short neighboring-module path. Photonic links distribute entanglement between stationary modules and are subject to photon collection, detection, buffering, and heralding probabilities. The two mechanisms solve different distance and packaging problems.

Universal Quantum’s partnership with Atlas Copco also emphasizes long-term vacuum stability, background-gas collision suppression, fast transport, serviceability, and manufacturability as prerequisites for synchronizing thousands of qubits. The company’s machine is a roadmap and engineering program, not a demonstrated utility-scale system.

### 2.5 Academic and networked demonstrations

Several academic results provide important primitives even when they are not complete commercial machines.

Pino and colleagues’ 2021 Nature experiment integrated a scalable surface trap, multiple interaction zones, parallel operations, fast transport, mid-circuit measurement, and a teleported CNOT with negligible reported crosstalk error. The system reached quantum volume 64. The authors explicitly stated that engineering low-error operations across multiple zones had slowed QCCD scaling, which remains an accurate description of the problem ([2021 QCCD demonstration](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03318-4)).

The 2023 Race-Track processor used a linear-trap QCCD with periodic boundary conditions, electrode broadcasting, multilayer RF routing, and magneto-optical-trap loading. It initially operated with 32 qubits and demonstrated a 32-qubit GHZ state, Hamiltonian simulation, QAOA, repetition-code error correction, and qubit-reuse experiments ([Race-Track processor](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevx.13.041052)).

Grid-based QCCD is intended to increase routing flexibility and wiring efficiency. A 2024 experiment used translationally symmetric electrode co-wiring and a binary-gated voltage exchange so that site-dependent operations required a fixed number of analogue signals plus one digital input per site. In two nominally identical grid traps, conditional reordering and adjacent-site exchange reached a 2.5-kilohertz exchange rate with sub-quantum axial motional excitation ([grid-based transport](https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevX.14.041028)).

Photonic networking has progressed in distance and in protocol complexity. A 2023 experiment connected calcium ions in separate buildings 230 metres apart using 520(2) metres of optical fiber ([elementary ion network](https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.050803)). A 2025 network-node experiment generated up to 44 time-bin modes across 12 kilometres of fiber, achieving 4.28 remote ion-photon entanglement events per second against a memory-decoherence rate of 3.69 per second. The final heralded ion-photon fidelity was $`89.8(1.1)\%`$, and wavelength conversion efficiency was 12%, compared with a cited current best of 57% ([12-kilometre network node](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67311-5)).

These are network-node achievements rather than multi-module fault-tolerant processors. Their importance is that they expose the practical requirements—phase stability, conversion, memory lifetime, detector efficiency, and multiplexing—that a useful network must solve.

Finally, a September 2026 experiment reported distributed error detection and correction between two separate trapped-ion processors. Entanglement between network qubits enabled remote syndrome measurements on data qubits; the demonstration implemented a distributed $`[[2,1,1]]`$ repetition code and real-time feed-forward correction of arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state ([distributed QEC demonstration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13065)). This is a major transition from distributing entanglement to using entanglement for computation, but it remains a two-processor, small-code experiment.

## 3. Proposed ion-trap scaling strategies

The proposals are best understood as a stack rather than mutually exclusive alternatives. Trap geometry determines where ions can move; control technology determines how gates and measurements are delivered; interconnect technology determines how modules communicate; and the error-correction architecture determines how physical imperfections become logical performance.

### 3.1 Single-chain and monolithic growth

The simplest strategy is to increase the number of ions in one crystal and preserve all-to-all connectivity through collective motional modes. It is attractive because it avoids physical interconnects and routing between modules. It also exploits a central trapped-ion strength: arbitrary pairs can interact without the swap networks required by nearest-neighbor superconducting processors.

The problem is that the same collective mode that supplies connectivity becomes harder to control as the chain grows. A 2024 shuttling analysis states that gate speed in a single trap decreases approximately as $`1/\sqrt{N}`$ with ion count $`N`$, exposing longer operations to background errors. Long chains also contain more motional modes, making mode calibration, spectator-mode suppression, and parallel operations increasingly difficult ([shuttling analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.14065v2)).

This route is therefore useful as a small-register architecture and as a local memory or processing unit, but it is unlikely to be the sole path to thousands of high-throughput qubits. Optical-tweezer segmentation and global-control proposals attempt to preserve the physical simplicity of one long chain while localizing modes and parallelizing gates.

### 3.2 Segmented QCCD with local shuttling

QCCD divides a processor into memory, logic, cooling, loading, and measurement zones. Ions are split, transported, merged for a gate, separated again, and rearranged into new groups. The 2021 QCCD paper summarized the mechanism precisely: maintain the low error rates of small ion crystals by limiting interactions to manageable groups, then physically rearrange ions into new crystals for subsequent interactions.

QCCD’s advantages are substantial:

- it preserves high local gate fidelity;
- it supports all-to-all logical connectivity through movement;
- it allows memory and processing zones to be specialized;
- it naturally supports mid-circuit measurement and reset;
- it can exploit ion loss detection and sympathetic cooling;
- and it provides a path from one processor to multiple modules.

Its costs are transport time, motional excitation, junction engineering, voltage waveform generation, cooling, and control bandwidth. The 2022 matter-link experiment demonstrated the core primitive between two neighboring modules, but multi-module QEC requires transport schedules, link calibration, and recovery that are much more demanding than a two-module demonstration.

QCCD can be implemented in linear, racetrack, grid, circular, or folded geometries. The geometry changes routing overhead and wiring, but does not change the basic physical mechanism.

### 3.3 Grid, ring, and circular QCCD

Grid QCCD increases routing flexibility by providing multiple paths and junctions. The 2024 grid-trap experiment demonstrated sub-quantum excitation during adjacent-site exchanges and showed that electrode broadcasting can reduce the number of unique analogue control lines. Its current control logic was software-based; the proposed hardware crossover switches and large integrated arrays remain future work.

Circular or ring-based QCCD designs reduce the movement and wiring cost of repeated cyclic operations. The 2026 Cyclone analysis proposes moving ancilla qubits in lockstep around a flexible ring rather than using a conventional two-dimensional grid. It reports up to fourfold modeled execution-time improvement, fewer traps and junctions, and a constant DAC count rather than a count that grows linearly with grid size ([Cyclone analysis](https://doi.org/10.1109/hpca68181.2026.11408498)).

These approaches are promising because their optimization target is concrete: reduce transport distance, junction count, and DAC growth while preserving parallelism. Their limitation is evidentiary. Cyclone and related ring proposals are software-hardware analyses, not demonstrations of a large fault-tolerant processor.

### 3.4 Optical-tweezer segmentation of long chains

Optical-tweezer architectures add local optical potentials to a long ion chain. The tweezers segment an arbitrarily long crystal into cells with localized phonon modes, allowing gates within different cells to run in parallel while retaining the possibility of reconfiguring the whole chain.

Olsacher and colleagues proposed programmable optical tweezers that localize motional modes to small subsets of ions. The analysis covered long one-dimensional chains and even infinite uniformly spaced chains, but it was theoretical rather than a large-chain experimental fidelity demonstration ([optical-tweezer mode localization](https://doi.org/10.1103/prxquantum.1.020316)).

A 2024 PRX proposal extends the idea to dynamically operated tweezers that create manageable cells, support parallel gates, enable mid-circuit measurement and feedback, and compensate crosstalk. It does not report measured fidelity, throughput, or manufacturing performance in the arbitrarily long regime ([segmented long-chain proposal](https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevX.14.041017)).

The route could reduce the number of hard-wired trap junctions, but it shifts complexity into high-power, phase-stable, dynamically controlled optical potentials. It is therefore a conditional alternative to QCCD, not a demonstrated replacement.

### 3.5 Fixed modules with photonic interconnects

A fixed-module architecture keeps each ion register small and connects modules by photons. Local gates use native ion interactions; inter-module gates use heralded entanglement, teleportation, lattice surgery, or distributed error correction. The 2014 modular architecture showed that such a hierarchy could be fault tolerant for modest circuits ([modular atomic-memory architecture](https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.89.022317)).

The advantage is scalability beyond the size, yield, and wiring limit of one chip. Modules can be fabricated, tested, replaced, and perhaps upgraded independently. Long-distance links also allow a system to be laid out like a network rather than a single monolithic device.

The disadvantage is that remote entanglement is probabilistic and slow compared with local gates. Collection optics, photon loss, detector dark counts, phase noise, frequency conversion, buffering, and distillation all consume resources. A photonic link must be judged by rate, density, fidelity, distance, and mapping latency simultaneously; optimizing one quantity can worsen the others.

### 3.6 Hybrid matter-link and photonic networks

The most plausible very-large system is hierarchical:

- local two-qubit gates within small ion crystals;
- deterministic matter links between neighboring chips or zones;
- photonic links between more distant modules;
- quantum memories and buffers that hide link latency;
- and a compiler that treats remote entanglement as a scarce resource.

The 2022 matter-link experiment points toward this division of labor. It found that neighboring-module ion transport was fast and deterministic, while photonic links had lower rates and fidelity. The same study suggested that shared optical cavities might support microsecond-scale interactions over a limited scale, after which slower photonic links would be needed for further expansion.

This hybrid route has the best architectural logic, but it requires a clean interface between matter transport, photonic network qubits, data qubits, and error-correction blocks. A photonic Bell pair generated at the edge of a module is not useful until it is mapped onto the data qubits that participate in QEC.

### 3.7 Control and I/O strategies

Control strategies are orthogonal to the trap geometry. A QCCD can use lasers, integrated photonics, electronic control, or a mixture.

| Control strategy | Scaling mechanism | Representative evidence | Main advantage | Main unresolved issue |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bulk laser addressing | Individual beams or acousto-optic deflection control ions | IonQ Forte and conventional QCCD systems | Highest demonstrated fidelity and mature control toolbox | Optical alignment, power, beam count, and crosstalk |
| Trap-integrated photonics | Waveguides, grating couplers, modulators, and photonic routing distribute light on-chip | Two-zone integrated-photonic QCCD; photonic modulator experiments | Reduces free-space alignment and can support dense optical I/O | Dielectric-induced motional shifts, loss, UV materials, drift, monolithic fabrication |
| Electronic or microwave control | RF antennas and local electrodes generate gate fields directly on the chip | Oxford Ionics seven-zone device; EQC prototypes | Reduces individually addressed gate beams and improves wiring scalability | RF crosstalk, thermal dissipation, spatial selectivity, scale-up of fidelity |
| WISE/global control | Integrated switching electronics multiplex a small number of complex external signals | 1,000-qubit, 200-control-line architecture proposal | Orders-of-magnitude reduction in external wiring | Restrictive interface may reduce QEC throughput |
| MAGIC or related RF-gradient control | Radio-frequency fields and magnetic gradients replace laser-driven gates | Industry architecture proposal | Potentially commodity-electronics manufacturing | Large-system performance data unavailable |

The 2023 WISE proposal illustrates the wiring opportunity: it describes a 1,000-qubit fully connected design operated with approximately 200 control lines using existing classes of chips and infrastructure ([WISE](https://journals.aps.org/prxquantum/abstract/10.1103/PRXQuantum.4.040313)). That is an architectural feasibility claim, not a 1,000-qubit experimental operation.

The 2026 WISER design-space exploration adds an important counterweight. It finds a narrow feasible global-control region requiring two-ion traps, moderate multiplexing, aggressive recooling, and high-rate qLDPC codes. Even assuming approximately tenfold physical-error improvement, its lower-bound cycle time to reach logical error below $`10^{-8}`$ is about 100 milliseconds, approximately three times slower than local-control QCCD in the modeled comparison. WISE may therefore be worthwhile when wiring is the binding constraint, but local control has the stronger modeled throughput position ([WISER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13546)).

### 3.8 Error-correction layers

Hardware architecture and QEC architecture must be co-designed.

Surface codes are comparatively mature and have well-developed decoders and threshold analyses, but their physical-qubit overhead and communication requirements can be large. Color-code and lattice-surgery layouts can exploit ion-trap connectivity, but distributed operations require high-rate links.

Quantum LDPC codes offer higher encoding rates. The Walking Cat $`[[102,22,9]]`$, $`[[70,6,9]]`$, and $`[[54,2,10]]`$ examples use moving ions, cat states, magic factories, and a streaming decoder. The modeled advantage is considerable, but the architecture assumes a collection of components that have only been demonstrated separately or at much smaller scale.

Distributed QEC adds a second layer of requirements. A 2026 remote lattice-surgery analysis reports that seam errors can tolerate substantially more noise than bulk errors in some protocols, but a syndrome round consumes $`O(d)`$ Bell pairs and a complete logical operation can consume $`O(d^2)`$ pairs when repeated over $`O(d)`$ rounds ([distributed lattice surgery](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2603.06513)). The link, code, and workload must therefore be selected together.

## 4. Technical feasibility and implementation barriers

### 4.1 Trap fabrication, vacuum, and packaging

#### Chip scale and fabrication yield

A surface-electrode QCCD is more than a set of electrodes. It must integrate trap electrodes, insulating layers, RF and DC routing, optical access, loading structures, junctions, possibly photonic waveguides, and sometimes RF antennas. As the array grows, microscopic variations in electrode dimensions and dielectric surfaces produce variations in trap frequencies, micromotion, heating, and gate calibration.

A 2022 footprint analysis estimated that a 90-by-90-millimetre array fabricated on a 150-millimetre silicon wafer, containing 1,296 X-junctions and up to 20 ions per junction, could hold about $`2.6\times10^4`$ qubits. The same analysis concluded that incorporating such a count into one practical QCCD would not be realistic without networking modules because area, yield, wiring, and control complexity become limiting.

Alternative electrode geometries illustrate the manufacturing trade-off. A 2025 simulation framework compared surface, grounded-surface, and cross-RF traps. Under one specified 40Ca+ operating point, the simulated cross-RF design reduced normalized power dissipation by approximately four orders of magnitude relative to a surface-trap reference and had greater simulated trap depth, while grounded-surface designs were intermediate. The paper also judged cross-RF fabrication especially difficult, with grounded-surface geometry a more plausible near-term balance ([trap-geometry framework](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.00218v1)).

These are simulations, not production data. No supplied source reports validated manufacturing yield, defect distributions, wafer-to-wafer variation, or the cost of discarding failed chips at 1,000 or 10,000 physical qubits.

#### Vacuum and thermal operation

Ion traps require extreme vacuum to suppress collisions and maintain stable ion chains. A 2026 systems-integration guide gives a conventional target below $`10^{-11}`$ mbar and a 150–200°C bake lasting from days to weeks. It estimates 10–16 weeks from a lab-ready facility to first useful operations and warns that a leak can restart bake-out and commissioning ([systems-integration guide](https://postquantum.com/building-quantum-computers/building-trapped-ion-quantum-computer/)). These are guide-level estimates, not a standardized industry measurement.

Cryogenic operation reduces background-gas collisions and anomalous electric-field noise but complicates wiring, optical access, thermal budgets, repair, and recooling. The Walking Cat model assumes cryogenic QCCD operation and explicitly includes ion loss, leakage, cooling, and replenishment. Universal Quantum’s DLR architecture instead targets approximately 70 K, arguing that moderate cooling simplifies thermal management and may reduce ion heating and loss. The supplied DLR material does not provide measured heating, loss, or gate-error values demonstrating that benefit.

The engineering decision is not simply “room temperature versus cryogenic.” It is a system trade-off among vacuum lifetime, electrode noise, photonic and electronic integration, heat extraction, serviceability, and power per logical qubit.

#### Packaging and serviceability

A 2021 trapped-ion demonstrator occupied two 19-inch racks, used modular replaceable parts, and required one wall-mounted power connection. This showed that a complete ion-trap system can be packaged as a data-centre-like appliance rather than a purely optical laboratory, but it remained a demonstrator and required further hardware and software upgrades before broad cloud deployment ([rack-scale demonstrator](https://doi.org/10.1103/prxquantum.2.020343)).

At utility scale, serviceability becomes a correctness issue. If one module fails, the system must either isolate it, replace it, or continue with degraded capacity. In a cryogenic machine, warming and recooling a failed module can interrupt the whole system. A modular vacuum architecture with independent service zones is more maintainable but introduces interfaces that must preserve low collision rates and stable optical alignment.

### 4.2 Optical control, integrated photonics, and electronic control

#### Laser scaling

Conventional laser control has produced the best demonstrated ion-trap fidelities, but every additional addressed ion adds demands on beam delivery, frequency stabilization, polarization, intensity control, alignment, and calibration. Acousto-optic deflectors and individual beam steering can make small systems flexible, but they do not remove the physical requirement to deliver stable optical power to many locations.

The optical-I/O mismatch is fundamental: qubit count grows approximately with chip area, whereas edge-coupled optical I/O grows with chip perimeter. A 2023 integrated-photonics analysis proposes on-chip amplitude and phase modulators so one optical launch can fan out through waveguide splitters to many ion-addressing lines. That shifts part of the problem into electrical control, but still requires a unique electrical signal per qubit ([integrated optical I/O](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41534-023-00737-1)).

A separate piezoelectric Mach–Zehnder modulator switched in less than one microsecond, achieved 38.7 dB extinction, and controlled a single 40Ca+ ion with single-qubit fidelity above 99.7% by gate-set tomography. Long-term tests revealed that the switching voltage drifted from 24 V to 46 V over several months, although periodic retuning preserved extinction. This is a useful component result and an equally useful warning: a device can meet a short experiment’s fidelity target while remaining unsuitable for unattended production without calibration recovery.

#### Trap-integrated photonics

Trap-integrated photonics can distribute control light, collect fluorescence, and form photonic interconnects on or below the trap chip. A 2025 PRX experiment demonstrated the first transport and coherent multizone operation in an integrated-photonic ion trap: one ion was transported between two zones while controlled optically, and two ions in separate zones were controlled simultaneously with little interference ([integrated-photonic QCCD](https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevX.15.011040)).

The experiment also identified a direct integration problem. Exposed dielectric surfaces from photonic structures disturbed ion motion during transport, requiring compensation in each zone and between zones. This calibration burden will grow with the number of zones and with photonic-material variation.

Simulation of a three-ion photonic circuit predicts beam waists of 4.3 micrometres axially and 2.2 micrometres transversely, with simulated crosstalk of −20 to −30 dB at 5–8 micrometre separations. Adding a 50-nanometre ITO layer reduced simulated focusing efficiency by about 10% because of absorption and interference ([photonic addressing design](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44310-025-00102-4)). The values are design simulations rather than a demonstration of an integrated, large-scale optical-control layer.

#### Electronic and microwave control

EQC directly attacks the number of optical control channels. Oxford Ionics’ seven-zone experiment shows that electronic control can deliver high fidelity and site selectivity in a real multi-zone trap. Universal Quantum’s architecture adds global fields, ASICs, and low-noise DACs to reduce the growth of individual control lines.

Electronic control introduces its own constraints:

- RF fields must be shaped to suppress coupling into neighboring zones;
- local ion positioning must remain accurate;
- antenna and electrode fabrication variations must be calibrated;
- shared antennas may support all single-qubit or all two-qubit operations in parallel, but not arbitrary mixtures;
- power dissipated near the trap must be removed without degrading vacuum or ion stability;
- microwave and RF signals must not create additional motional heating or AC Zeeman shifts.

The Walking Cat microarchitecture explicitly assumes EQC because it reduces the laser-power burden and enables parallel operations. Its model reports single-qubit operations in 5–10 microseconds, entangling drives in 100–300 microseconds, and transport in 5–15 microseconds, but these are component-level or assumed operating ranges rather than a complete thousands-qubit demonstration.

### 4.3 Ion transport, motional heating, and junctions

Transport is the defining advantage and defining cost of QCCD.

The 2022 matter-link experiment moved 174Yb+ and 171Yb+ ions between two surface-electrode QCCD modules over 684 micrometres at 2,424 transfers per second. Ion-loss infidelity was below $`7\times10^{-8}`$, and 15 million consecutive links succeeded in a transport-loss test. Ramsey measurements found no measurable loss of phase coherence after 100 inter-module links over a 100-millisecond delay; the data implied an upper bound of $`5\times10^{-4}`$ infidelity per link. Transport speed was limited by DAC update rate and DC-filter bandwidth, and the paper identified faster DACs, higher filter cutoffs, or predistorted waveforms as routes to another order of magnitude improvement.

This is strong evidence for neighboring-module transport, but the requirements become harder when transport is repeated inside QEC. Ions acquire phonons during motion, junctions reduce confinement, and merging or splitting can transfer motional energy into data ions. A 2026 compiler analysis cites literature reports of 37–150 axial motional quanta per traverse through Y-junctions while noting that newer experiments have improved performance ([robust ion shuttling](https://www.cda.cit.tum.de/files/eda/2026_qsw_robust_ion_shuttling.pdf)).

The grid-trap experiment’s 2.5-kilohertz exchange with sub-quantum excitation is encouraging, but it does not establish that arbitrary long-distance routing through a large grid can operate at that rate. QCCD control must also recover from defects. In a simulated 5-by-5 grid with 40% random junction defects, a hybrid cycle–path reconfiguration strategy achieved 100% success at 50%, 75%, and 100% occupancy, with normalized overheads of 1.08, 1.16, and 1.30 in ten-run evaluations. Cycle-only and path-only strategies failed in some occupancy regimes. This demonstrates software robustness under a model, not hardware reliability at that defect rate.

Transport also interacts with dynamical decoupling. A 2026 H2 study found that increasing decoupling-pulse frequency beyond 2 Hz was generally counterproductive in its modeled regime because scheduling errors injected dephasing. With empirical compiler timing characterized by mean $`2(1)\times10^{-4}`$ seconds and standard deviation $`4.8(1)\times10^{-3}`$ seconds, additional pulses could trade environmental protection for control-induced noise ([QCCD dynamical decoupling study](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.14441v1)).

This is why “fast transport” is not enough. The acceptance criterion is low motional excitation after repeated transport, junction passage, merge, split, gate, cooling, and reconfiguration operations, with calibration recovery after changes in ion number and species.

### 4.4 Crosstalk and calibration

Crosstalk arises through several mechanisms:

- optical spillover between neighboring ions;
- RF or microwave fields extending beyond the intended zone;
- shared motional modes during simultaneous gates;
- laser scatter and detector contamination;
- DAC waveform distortion;
- calibration drift in trap frequencies, micromotion, field gradients, and phase references.

A 2024 fault-tolerance analysis emphasizes that parallel entangling gates are essential for large systems but that collective motional modes make crosstalk particularly damaging. It proposes programmable optical-tweezer pulse optimization to suppress crosstalk below a code-specific threshold, but the extracted result does not include a measured below-threshold demonstration ([parallel-gate crosstalk analysis](https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevApplied.22.034021)).

A 2025 pulse-optimization preprint numerically reduces a heating-error estimate at 44 ions from $`2.18\times10^{-3}`$ for a conventional method to $`4.56\times10^{-4}`$, about a fivefold reduction. However, direct infidelity calculations were limited to systems of six or fewer ions; for larger systems the work uses an upper-bound estimator because the Hilbert-space dimension grows exponentially ([heating-aware pulse optimization](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.13457)). It is therefore a useful control proposal, not evidence that a 44-ion processor has achieved the estimated fidelity.

Calibration must become automated and hierarchical. A useful large system will need:

- local calibration of every zone and junction;
- continuous monitoring of motional frequencies and micromotion;
- crosstalk characterization under simultaneous operation;
- automatic recalibration after loading, loss, or transport;
- model-based scheduling that avoids unstable combinations;
- fault isolation when a zone becomes unusable;
- and calibration metadata that the compiler can consume.

The supplied evidence contains promising scheduling and control studies, but no common end-to-end benchmark reports calibration time, recovery time, or fraction of uptime across competing architectures.

### 4.5 Photonic interconnects: the main modular bottleneck

A useful photonic link must satisfy three conditions at once:

1. sufficient Bell-pair rate;
2. sufficient Bell-pair fidelity;
3. sufficient channel density to fit alongside the QPU.

For a module that needs $`B`$ Bell pairs per syndrome cycle of duration $`\tau_{\mathrm{syndrome}}`$, the minimum average link rate is $`R_{\mathrm{link}}\geq B/\tau_{\mathrm{syndrome}}`$. The rate requirement changes sharply with code and cycle time.

| Fault-tolerant interface | Bell pairs per cycle in cited model | Syndrome cycle | Required rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Surface-code transversal interface | 729 pairs for distance 27 | 1 ms | $`7.29\times10^5`$ pairs/s |
| Surface-code transversal interface | 729 pairs for distance 27 | 55 ms | $`1.33\times10^4`$ pairs/s |
| qLDPC surgery interface | approximately 40–80 pairs | 1 ms | approximately $`8.0\times10^4`$ pairs/s |
| qLDPC surgery interface | approximately 40–80 pairs | 55 ms | approximately $`1.5\times10^3`$ pairs/s |

These estimates come from the 2026 modular-link analysis and depend on code distance, adapter, and syndrome schedule ([remote-link resource analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.18387)). They show why qLDPC surgery can reduce the immediate link-rate burden, while a fast surface-code cycle demands far denser interconnects.

The measured baseline is far below the aggressive target. The 2026 Perspective states that the best demonstrated trapped-ion heralded links reach about 97% fidelity at up to 250 pairs per second, whereas local entangling operations exceed 99.99% at approximately $`10^4`$ operations per second. A 2022 comparison reported 182 entanglement connections per second at 94% fidelity and estimated that switching, wavelength conversion, and distillation could reduce effective rate to about one pair per second.

A proposed Bell factory changes the scaling law by using single-photon rather than two-photon heralding. Two-photon coincidence success scales quadratically with collection efficiency; single-photon heralding scales linearly. The proposal combines this with integrated photonics, coherent recoil correction, leakage detection, and one round of projective distillation.

Using 88Sr+ and modeled parameters, it projects:

- 896 distilled Bell pairs per second per channel with an infinite buffer;
- 858 pairs per second per channel with a four-ion buffer and modeled starvation;
- approximately $`1.0\times10^5`$ pairs per second per square centimetre;
- modeled delivered fidelity near 99.96%, with a target above 99.9%.

The design uses a 237-nanosecond attempt cycle, 0.5% end-to-end detection probability, and six QCCD zones per channel. Crucially, it delivers the Bell pair to the edge of the QPU; mapping that pair onto data qubits is excluded. The result is therefore the most quantitatively specified photonic-interconnect proposal in the supplied evidence, but it remains a projection ([Bell-factory proposal](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.18387)).

The proposal’s success depends on components that are individually plausible but not yet demonstrated together: UV switches with high extinction, low-loss integrated collection, stable phase references, detector dark-count suppression, dense channel routing, and fast local distillation. The bottleneck may shift from photon collection to local gates, but it does not disappear.

### 4.6 Error correction, decoding, and feed-forward

#### Physical-to-logical overhead

The National Academies gave a generic historical example in which average error rates needed to fall by 10–100 times before error correction could work reliably at scale, followed by at least a $`10^5`$-fold increase in physical qubits to create a useful number of effective logical qubits. Modern codes and hardware have changed the numerical estimates, but the basic lesson remains: improving fidelity and increasing qubit count must happen together.

The relevant logical target is application-dependent. The supplied architecture studies use logical error targets from approximately $`10^{-3}`$ for early applications to $`10^{-9}`$, $`10^{-10}`$, or lower for long computations. The generic 99% threshold in a 2020 review is not a substitute for a code-specific threshold; a remote link, a local gate, a syndrome measurement, and a complete logical operation can have different tolerances.

For a simplified sub-threshold model, the logical error per cycle is often written as $`p_L\approx\kappa(p/p_{\mathrm{th}})^{(d+1)/2}`$, giving $`d\approx2\ln(\kappa V)/\ln(p_{\mathrm{th}}/p)-1`$ when total circuit spacetime volume $`V`$ must remain reliable. This expression is a model, not a universal law. It illustrates why code distance grows only logarithmically with workload volume but why the physical error must remain below threshold with margin.

#### QLDPC and cat-state architectures

Walking Cat’s modeled QLDPC system is notable because it includes the entire stack:

- memory blocks;
- cat factories;
- magic-state factories;
- Bell factories;
- qubit-loss replenishment;
- compiler;
- logical instruction set;
- and streaming decoder.

Its $`[[102,22,9]]`$ block has higher logical density than the cited surface-code comparison. A modeled 110-logical-qubit configuration uses 2,514 physical qubits and produces approximately one million T gates per day at a target logical error of $`10^{-10}`$. A larger configuration uses 7,559 physical qubits for 220 logical qubits and more than ten million T gates per day.

The architecture accounts for leakage and ion loss, which many high-level resource estimates omit. In its moving-qubit model, a Q102 memory block uses 316 physical qubits, has a modeled logical error rate of approximately $`10^{-11}`$ per syndrome extraction cycle, and requires approximately 33.7 physical-operation cycles per syndrome cycle. The Q70 block uses 220 physical qubits and has modeled logical error around $`10^{-10}`$ per cycle. These values rely on assumed physical error $`p=10^{-4}`$, loss $`10^{-7}`$, leakage $`10^{-5}`$, and a 200-microsecond physical-operation cycle.

The decoder is also modeled rather than demonstrated on a full machine. For one million simulated syndrome cycles, the Q70 streaming decoder has mean decoding time per cycle of approximately 0.147 milliseconds and 99.9th percentile of 0.326 milliseconds; Q102 has mean approximately 0.397 milliseconds and 99.9th percentile approximately 1.494 milliseconds. These results show that real-time decoding is plausible under the model, but they do not establish processor-wide classical-control latency.

#### Real-time control

QuCtrl-BELL provides a useful hardware-level example. A nine-slot chassis supports up to 24 DDS/AWG outputs and 32 TTL channels, with local RISC-V boards executing step tables at 4-nanosecond clock resolution. It measured below 100 nanoseconds for fixed TTL-readout or broadcast delay and below 700 nanoseconds for end-to-end read-TTL feedback. The authors caution that approximately 700 nanoseconds per feedback event may become a bottleneck for rapid multi-round QEC ([QuCtrl-BELL](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.22433v1)).

This board-level latency is not the same as end-to-end measurement latency. A 2025 trapped-ion fluorescence-classification study found that an FPGA implementation reduced complete one- and three-qubit detection latency to approximately 1.78 and 2.29 milliseconds, compared with about 212 and 215 milliseconds for a GPU path. The accelerator itself contributed little of the GPU latency; approximately 98% arose from the PCIe-rooted interface. The result demonstrates that data movement and camera interfaces may dominate the machine’s feedback loop even when the classifier is fast ([FPGA fluorescence readout](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.15838)).

Useful fault tolerance therefore requires a control architecture that co-designs:

- detector and camera exposure;
- data movement;
- local state classification;
- syndrome decoding;
- logical-frame updates;
- feed-forward;
- and transport scheduling.

### 4.7 Manufacturing, supply chain, cost, and workforce

The industrialization question has four distinct parts:

1. Can trap chips and control electronics be fabricated reproducibly?
2. Can lasers, photonic components, RF electronics, detectors, and vacuum packages be supplied in volume?
3. Can systems be assembled, calibrated, and maintained with predictable labor?
4. Can the resulting cost and energy per logical qubit support deployment?

Current evidence answers only the first part partially. Quantinuum’s 300-millimetre program is a serious step toward semiconductor-style fabrication, but yields and production volumes remain undisclosed. Oxford Ionics reports commercial sales and field-upgradeable systems, but its large-scale roadmap is not a production validation.

The systems-integration guide estimates 4–6 full-time staff for a research deployment and 6–10 plus vendor support for a production service, with laser specialists particularly difficult to recruit. It also estimates 1.5-by-3-metre optical tables for conventional systems and warns that a 1°C shift can disturb cavity locking. These figures are useful planning inputs but are not globally standardized measurements.

Publicly comparable total-cost, power, maintenance, uptime, and energy-per-logical-qubit measurements are unavailable. IonQ has correctly identified cost and energy per logical qubit, plus cost and time to solution, as the metrics that determine real-world value, but the supplied evidence does not report these metrics for a completed useful workload ([IonQ value metrics](https://www.roic.ai/quote/IONQ/transcripts/2026-year/2-quarter)).

This is a major uncertainty in all rankings. A route that reaches 10,000 physical qubits but requires a dedicated team of specialists per module, frequent vacuum intervention, and large laser-power infrastructure may lose to a route with fewer logical qubits but much higher uptime and lower operating cost.

## 5. From scaled hardware to real-world workloads

### 5.1 Near-term applications are not fault-tolerant utility

Trapped ions already support small chemistry, optimization, machine-learning, and benchmarking demonstrations. A 2018 experiment used up to four calcium ions to estimate the ground-state energy of molecular hydrogen and lithium hydride with a variational quantum eigensolver. It provided an important proof of concept but also showed that measurement noise and mitigation were central limitations ([four-qubit chemistry demonstration](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevx.8.031022)).

IonQ reports a cargo-loading optimization experiment with Airbus, an electronic-structure simulation with AstraZeneca, AWS, and NVIDIA, and an eight-qubit road-sign classifier with Hyundai. The company reports a 656-fold chemistry acceleration, but the supplied information does not give the problem size, baseline runtime, independent replication, or deployment result. These examples show application engagement, not independently validated quantum advantage.

Quantinuum’s H2 product is offered through direct subscription and Microsoft Azure access for chemistry, materials, finance, logistics, and transportation. This is important for access and software development, but vendor application positioning is not equivalent to a completed workload with a classical baseline and total cost.

The strongest supplied application-level evidence is Microsoft and Quantinuum’s 12-logical-qubit hybrid chemistry calculation, which estimated a catalytic-intermediate ground-state energy at chemical accuracy using logical qubits, AI, and HPC. It is a meaningful step toward a scientific workflow, but it does not yet provide the wall-clock, energy, cost, and independent baseline needed to establish commercial advantage.

### 5.2 Resource estimates define the engineering target

Three workload estimates clarify the gap between current demonstrations and useful fault tolerance.

| Workload | Resource estimate | Evidence status | What it implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ru-based catalyst chemistry | 1 mHa target; 1.8 million physical qubits and one-day ion-trap runtime for a 56-orbital/64-electron system; larger cases require 3.7–5.7 million physical qubits | Full-stack model compared with SHCI | Chemistry utility may require millions of physical qubits and complete algorithmic, QEC, and hardware co-design |
| Heisenberg simulation | 162 logical qubits and approximately 10,000 physical qubits for a 100-site model, including shots for chemical accuracy; estimated one-month runtime | Walking Cat architecture estimate | A few thousand logical-capable physical qubits could enter a classically difficult simulation regime if the model assumptions hold |
| secp256k1 ECDLP | Approximately 1,450 logical qubits, 40 million Toffoli gates, 19,397 physical qubits, 25.7 days, 63% estimated success | Architecture-specific preprint estimate | A cryptographically meaningful task may require tens of thousands rather than millions of physical qubits under aggressive qLDPC and compiler optimization |

The catalyst estimate targets the ground-state energy of a ruthenium catalyst compound to 1 millihartree. The authors emphasize that the chosen energy difference is a proxy for a sub-reaction and that further calculations are needed for the complete catalytic cycle. For the 56-orbital/64-electron case, the model gives one day on an ion-trap machine with 1.8 million physical qubits versus seven days for a classical SHCI calculation. Larger cases are estimated at 3.7 million and 5.7 million physical qubits ([full-stack catalyst co-design](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26547v1)).

The Walking Cat estimate is smaller because it uses a different workload, code family, error target, and architectural model. Its fast architecture estimates a one-month execution for a 100-site Heisenberg model using approximately 10,000 physical qubits and 162 logical qubits, including the shots required for chemical accuracy. Again, this is a modeled execution, not an executed experiment.

The ECDLP estimate is especially useful because it is compiled through a complete proposed stack. It includes a 31-fold improvement in CCZ execution time from a fast magic-state factory and depth-one injection, parallel cat-based measurements, logical Clifford optimization, loss correction, and reusable ancillas. Its 19,397-physical-qubit estimate is not a general requirement for every useful workload; it is the output of one architecture-specific compilation.

### 5.3 Surface codes, qLDPC codes, and the link budget

The choice of error-correction code changes the required physical system more than a simple physical-qubit count suggests.

A distance-27 surface-code interface can require 729 Bell pairs in one syndrome-extraction round for a transversal remote operation. A qLDPC surgery interface may use approximately 40–80 pairs per round but repeat the operation over multiple rounds. The surface-code approach demands a higher instantaneous rate; qLDPC surgery demands lower rate but more careful scheduling, bridging, and decoder coordination.

Remote lattice surgery studies find protocol-dependent Bell-pair thresholds. One 2026 analysis reports bulk-error thresholds around 1% and seam-error thresholds around 10% for an unrotated-code phenomenological model, with circuit-level values around 0.73% and 7.3% under a specified amplification factor. Other teleportation protocols report Bell-pair thresholds around 17–30% while local gate errors must remain roughly below 0.1–0.7%. These values are not universal; they depend on code, noise model, and protocol ([distributed lattice-surgery thresholds](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2603.06513)).

The practical conclusion is not that qLDPC automatically wins. qLDPC reduces encoding and link overhead in some designs, but it needs reliable nonlocal measurement, high-rate decoding, leakage and loss handling, and a compiler that respects its connectivity. Surface codes have more mature engineering and decoding ecosystems but may require much larger processors and denser links. The most likely progression is early QCCD systems using mature codes and later systems adopting higher-rate codes as the control and decoder stack becomes reliable.

### 5.4 Mapping each hardware strategy to useful workloads

#### Local QCCD

Local QCCD is best suited to workloads that benefit from high-fidelity all-to-all interactions and do not yet require a large number of modules. Chemistry, dense variational circuits, small error-correction experiments, and algorithms with deep interaction graphs can exploit its low routing overhead. The weakness is throughput: 55-millisecond operations layers and transport-plus-cooling overheads are much slower than isolated gate times.

#### QCCD with electronic control

Electronic control addresses the most obvious system bottlenecks—laser beam count, alignment, and power distribution. It is particularly valuable for a QCCD architecture with hundreds or thousands of zones, provided RF crosstalk and heat dissipation remain controlled. Its application advantage is indirect: it increases the probability that enough high-fidelity zones can be operated in parallel to support QEC.

#### QCCD with integrated photonics

Integrated photonics is valuable both for local laser addressing and for remote entanglement. It can reduce optical alignment and enable dense routing, but dielectric calibration, UV loss, phase stability, and process compatibility are central risks. A two-zone demonstration is an encouraging primitive; the required system is a photonic-electronic-vacuum stack with hundreds or thousands of repeated channels.

#### Fixed photonic modules

Fixed modules are the most natural route once a single QCCD chip becomes too large or too difficult to manufacture. They support independent fabrication and repair and can scale geographically. Their usefulness depends almost entirely on the link budget: rate, fidelity, density, buffer size, and data-qubit mapping must be measured together.

#### WISE and other global-control designs

Global-control architectures are attractive when wiring, not gate fidelity, is the dominant constraint. They could make a 1,000-qubit system physically connectable with far fewer external control lines. Their risk is that restrictive access to local operations may make syndrome extraction too slow. The WISER analysis suggests that global control is a conditional optimization, not an automatic replacement for local control.

#### Optical-tweezer and segmented-chain architectures

These approaches could reduce junction and chip-routing complexity while providing parallelism. Their strongest evidence is theoretical or simulated. They become credible competitors if they demonstrate long-chain gate fidelity, crosstalk below the relevant QEC threshold, rapid reconfiguration, and stable optical operation across hundreds of ions.

### 5.5 Access, deployment, and application measurement

A useful processor must be accessible to application developers. Cloud access through Azure and direct subscriptions lowers the barrier to experimentation, while field-upgradeable QPUs reduce the cost of replacing the quantum processor inside a deployed system. However, cloud availability does not establish useful quantum performance.

Every claimed application should report:

- the exact problem instance and input size;
- logical and physical qubit count;
- circuit depth and logical gate counts;
- number of samples;
- accuracy and confidence interval;
- wall-clock runtime;
- classical baseline and hardware;
- energy and cost where relevant;
- whether post-selection or error mitigation was used;
- and whether the result was independently reproduced.

The supplied evidence does not contain an independently validated, scaled ion-trap application reporting all of these quantities together. That absence limits the confidence of any claim that a current system already solves a real-world problem better than classical computing.

## 6. Comparative evaluation and likelihood of success

### 6.1 Common comparison

The following comparison uses measured results where available and labels proposals and models explicitly.

| Approach | Demonstrated basis | Connectivity and throughput | Integration burden | Provisional judgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Local segmented QCCD | Helios at 98 physical qubits; QCCD transport; Race-Track and grid demonstrations | All-to-all logical connectivity, but transport and cooling limit system clock | Junctions, DACs, motional heating, calibration, optical or RF zones | Strongest near-term physical scaling route |
| QCCD with EQC or integrated photonics | Seven-zone 99.97% EQC experiment; two-zone integrated-photonic QCCD | Potentially high parallelism and lower optical I/O burden; large-scale throughput unmeasured | RF crosstalk, dielectric effects, thermal operation, process compatibility | Most promising enabling complement |
| Fixed photonic modules | Long-distance ion networks, 97%-fidelity links, commercial two-system integration, distributed $`[[2,1,1]]`$ QEC | Potentially arbitrary module count; current rate and density far below aggressive QEC needs | Collection, detectors, phase, conversion, buffers, mapping, distillation | Necessary for very large systems but not yet utility-ready |
| Single-photon Bell factories | Projected 858–896 pairs/s/channel and $`10^5`$ pairs/s/cm² at about 99.9% fidelity | Designed to approach local-operation limits with dense parallel channels | UV switching, integrated collection, local distillation, data-qubit mapping | Best current photonic proposal; evidence remains modeled |
| WISE/global control | 1,000-qubit/200-line architecture proposal; WISER lower-bound study | Lower wiring complexity but modeled QEC cycle about 100 ms at $`\lt 10^{-8}`$ logical error | On-chip switching, constrained instruction interface, recooling | Conditional option when wiring dominates |
| Optical-tweezer segmentation | Long-chain localization and crosstalk proposals; no large-chain fidelity demonstration | Theoretical parallel cell operations and reconfigurable boundaries | High-power optical control, crosstalk, calibration, fabrication | Promising but lower current readiness |
| qLDPC/Walking Cat logical stack | Complete compiler, code, factory, decoder, and workload model | Modeled 100–220 logical qubits and millions of T gates/day | Requires thousands of physical qubits, low errors, reliable loss handling | Most compelling logical co-design; not yet hardware demonstrated |

### 6.2 Ranking the physical scaling routes

#### First: segmented QCCD with local shuttling

QCCD ranks first because its central scaling primitive is experimentally demonstrated at the relevant qualitative level. Helios shows that a nearly 100-qubit QCCD can preserve strong component fidelities across multiple zones. The matter-link experiment shows deterministic inter-module transport with very low ion-loss error. Grid, ring, and racetrack studies provide concrete paths to reduce wiring and routing overhead.

The confidence is high that QCCD will remain an important platform architecture. The confidence is lower that current QCCD implementations can reach useful fault-tolerant throughput without substantial changes to control electronics, cooling, code design, and module structure.

#### Second: QCCD combined with electronic control and integrated photonics

Electronic control and integrated photonics should not be ranked as wholly separate competitors. They address different parts of QCCD’s scaling problem. EQC reduces laser-addressing complexity; integrated photonics improves local optical delivery and remote entanglement; both can coexist with shuttling.

The evidence is strong for small or medium primitives and weak for large arrays. This combination is the most plausible medium-term route because it improves manufacturability without discarding QCCD’s demonstrated transport and connectivity advantages.

#### Third: hybrid matter-link and photonic modular systems

A very large machine will probably require photonic links even if local QCCD is the near-term backbone. Neighboring chips can exchange ions or use deterministic matter transport; longer-range modules can use photons. The hybrid architecture limits the number of high-performance remote links needed and allows local operations to dominate where possible.

It ranks below local QCCD for near-term feasibility because the photonic link must satisfy a stringent rate-density-fidelity budget. It ranks above purely monolithic or global-control routes for long-term scale because it is the only strategy in the supplied evidence that directly addresses module size, repair, and geographic expansion.

#### Fourth: WISE and other global-control architectures

WISE may solve the external-wiring problem at a lower hardware cost than fully local control.
